editorial:
Imagine stepping back into a time when computers were the size of refrigerators and animation was just starting to move away from hand-drawn sketches. You are looking at a piece of history here, a tiny window into the early days of computer graphics. This short is less about a complex plot and more about the pure joy of seeing shapes move in a way that felt like magic back in 1987. The vibe is very experimental and lighthearted, making you feel like you are hanging out in a digital lab watching a scientist play with new toys. 

What really sticks with you is how the shapes bounce and stretch, showing off those early physics rules that eventually led to the giant blockbusters we see today. While the graphics look blocky and simple now, the pacing is quick and it stays fun throughout. You should definitely check this out if you love tech history or animation. Since it is such a short piece, you can easily find it on digital archives or stream it in high definition on YouTube to see those polygons clearly. It is a great addition to any digital collection for fans of the craft.
endingExplained: The short ends by pushing the boundaries of the software to its limit. You see the main character and the environment react to physics in a way that was groundbreaking for the time. There is no big plot twist, but the climax is the successful demonstration of how a digital object can deform and move naturally. It wraps up by proving that computer animation could actually feel bouncy and alive rather than stiff.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves the history of CGI and early computer art.
